intro: Open a printed Hebrew Bible with commentaries and the verse sits in the middle of the page, surrounded by readers. Rashi, from eleventh-century France, explains a word. Ramban, from thirteenth-century Spain, answers him. A midrash compiled around 400 CE sits behind both. That page is the subject of this unit: how the Tanakh has been read, by whom, and with what questions. Jewish tradition treats the reading as a conversation that never closes, and this unit lets you listen in.

The first chapter follows Jewish interpretation from the rabbis of the midrash to Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak, Maimonides and the Zohar, and ends with the printed page that holds them together. The second chapter puts Jewish readers beside Christian and academic ones. It looks at Isaiah 7, Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Genesis 1, at the disputations of Paris and Barcelona, at modern dialogue, and at Spinoza, Wellhausen, the archaeologists and the literary and feminist critics. Nothing here decides which reading is true. Everything here describes what each reader saw and why.

By the end you will be able to sort a reading into peshat, remez, derash or sod; explain how Rashi and Ramban differ on the same verse; describe how a rabbi, a church father and a historian read Isaiah 53 without ranking them; and name the question each kind of reader is asking. That skill, telling questions apart, is what makes it possible to study a sacred text in a public school with respect for everyone in the room.
bigQuestion: How has one text been read so differently across a thousand years, and how can we describe those readings fairly without deciding which is true?

timeline.t: Genesis Rabbah is compiled in the Land of Israel; the rabbis' midrash on Genesis
The Babylonian Talmud reaches its final form, quoting verses on nearly every page
Rashi is born in Troyes; his commentaries become the standard companion to the text
Ibn Ezra leaves Spain and writes his grammar-based Torah commentary while traveling
Maimonides finishes the Guide of the Perplexed in Egypt, on the Torah's words for God
The Paris disputation; the Talmud is condemned and burned two years later
Ramban debates Pablo Christiani before King James I at Barcelona
The Zohar appears in Castile; Kabbalists name four levels of reading, PaRDeS
Daniel Bomberg prints the first Mikraot Gedolot in Venice; the 1525 edition sets the text
Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise opens critical study of who wrote the Torah
Wellhausen's Prolegomena gives the documentary hypothesis its classic form
Nostra Aetate; Jewish-Christian dialogue replaces disputation, as at Chicago in 1893

words.d: rabbinic interpretation that searches a verse for meaning; halakhah for law, aggadah for story
the plain sense of a verse in its context; the first of the four levels of reading
interpretation that goes beyond the plain sense, often through midrash
the acronym for the four levels of reading: peshat, remez, derash and sod
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki of Troyes (1040–1105), whose commentaries explain the plain sense and select fitting midrash
Nahmanides of Girona (1194–c. 1270), who debated Rashi and Ibn Ezra in his commentary and Pablo Christiani at Barcelona
Maimonides' work (c. 1190) reading the Torah's bodily language about God as figures of speech
the Rabbinic Bible, first printed in Venice in 1517, with the text in the center and commentaries around it
the list of books a community counts as scripture; the Tanakh has 24, a Protestant Old Testament 39
the Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14 rendered "the young woman" by JPS 1917 and "a virgin" by the KJV
a medieval debate ordered by a Christian ruler in which Jews had to defend their texts, as at Paris 1240 and Barcelona 1263
the theory, classically stated by Wellhausen in 1878, that the Torah was woven from sources J, E, D and P

test.q: Which kind of midrash fills gaps in the Torah's stories, such as Abraham's childhood?
test.why: Midrash aggadah, "telling," supplies stories for the text's silences; halakhah derives law.

test.q: What does Genesis Rabbah 1:1 say God looked into when creating the world?
test.why: The midrash reads "in the beginning" through Proverbs 8:22 and calls the Torah God's blueprint.

test.q: Which verse does Rabbi Joshua quote in the Talmud to reject a heavenly voice on a point of law?
test.why: "It is not in heaven," Deuteronomy 30:12, is quoted in Bava Metzia 59b.

test.q: What did Rashi say his commentary came to give, on Genesis 3:8?
choices: The plain sense and the aggadah that fits the words
test.why: Rashi states he came to give the peshat and the aggadah that settles the words in order.

test.q: Which commentator was born in Tudela and wandered through Italy, France and England after about 1140?
test.why: Ibn Ezra left Spain around 1140 and wrote his commentaries while traveling.

test.q: In the Guide of the Perplexed, how does Maimonides treat the Torah's mention of God's hand or face?
choices: As proof God has a body
As figures of speech in human language
test.why: Maimonides reads bodily language about God as figurative, since the Torah speaks in human language.
Sod is the secret level of meaning, the fourth in PaRDeS.

test.q: Who edited the 1525 Bomberg Rabbinic Bible whose text became the standard for centuries?
test.why: Jacob ben Hayyim edited the second Bomberg edition in Venice.

test.q: How many books does the Tanakh count?
test.why: The Tanakh counts 24 books, grouping Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah and the Twelve as one each.

test.q: Which book ends the Tanakh, and with what?
choices: Chronicles, with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem
test.why: The Ketuvim close with Chronicles and Cyrus's decree; the Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi.

test.q: How do Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak identify the servant of Isaiah 53?
test.why: The medieval Jewish commentators read the servant as Israel, despised in exile and then vindicated.

test.q: What did Ramban argue at Barcelona about aggadah?
choices: That it proves the Messiah has come
That it is the same as Talmudic law
That it should be translated into Latin
That Jews may accept or set aside aggadic stories
test.why: Ramban distinguished binding law and Tanakh from aggadah, which is not binding.

test.q: Which 1965 declaration rejected blaming Jews as a people for the death of Jesus?
test.why: Nostra Aetate, from the Second Vatican Council, rejected the collective charge and called for dialogue.

test.q: What did Spinoza's 1670 treatise say about the method for interpreting scripture?
choices: Interpret scripture from scripture, as one studies nature
test.why: Spinoza argued for building a history of each book from its text and language, like the study of nature.

test.q: What is the Tel Dan stele evidence for, according to most scholars?
choices: The exact date of the Exodus
The existence of a dynasty called the House of David
test.why: The 9th-century BCE inscription names the "House of David" but says nothing about David's life or kingdom.

write.prompt: Choose Isaiah 53:4, Genesis 1:26 or Genesis 1:1. State what the verse says in JPS 1917. Then present two readers from this unit (for example Rashi and Ramban, Rashi and Augustine, or Genesis Rabbah and a historian) and explain what question each asks and how each answers it from the text. Cite the verse and the reader by name. Close by saying what a fair description of both readings must include.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse, and the translation you quote.
Attribute every reading: "Rashi reads…", "Augustine reads…", "most historians hold…".
Say what question each reader is asking before you compare answers.
Compare; do not rank. Describe what each reading sees that the other does not.
Use the unit's terms: peshat, derash, sod, canon, disputation, documentary hypothesis.
